subject: Methods for grouping species for pooled detection function

messages.author: be2485b0836d6632
messages.subject: Methods for grouping species for pooled detection function
parts:
Dear all,

I'm working on estimating bird abundances from a dry forest in Peru, using line transect distance sampling, I have 20 species – of course some are more commonly recorded (c.1000 records) and others rarer (<200 records). My aim is to have density estimates by species by site (26 sites) over my study area.

I'm looking to combine species into groups sharing similar detectability so that I can use a pooled detection function for the less common species. The idea would be to have some more common species plus rarer species in each group, but this will depend on the outcome of my grouping.

As I understand it, to group species, they need to have similar detection functions, this could be approximated by charactersistics of detection such as maximum observed distance, as used by Alldredge et al 2007. I have considered using such characteristics influencing detectability – maybe getting several metrics and using a cluster analysis to find likely groups. But then I was thinking – why not use a test to compare distance distributions directly eg Anderson-Darling two sample, or Cramér–von Mises test (with emphasis on distances closer to 0) to compare the shape of the detection fall-off across species. Each pair of species would have a test statistic – and these pairwise ‘distance’ values (lower the statistic, the more similar  the distributions) could be fed into a cluster analysis to create the groups.

I'm also considering using covariates but would like to try this separately first, and then maybe compare approaches, or combine them.
I'd be interested to hear any opinions about potential problems in using this method. Apologies if this is not clear , please let me know.

Thanks for any guidance

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Methods for grouping species for pooled detection function
parts:
Christian:

About combining species for generating pooled detection functions.  I suspect the covariate approach is the one to use; it would allow you to "borrow strength" across species.  It is true you could do something like a K-S test of the respective detection histograms or more exotically conduct a cluster analysis.  However, place these analyses into some context:  you are doing an analysis (whether to combine) in anticipation of an analysis (detection function fitting) to produce an estimate of abundance.  I would suspect you will be looking for a more direct route to getting your analyses completed. 

As an aside, you are trying to produce 520 density estimates for each species X site combination.  That will be quite an achievement by itself.  I suspect you will be challenged to have sufficient data for all of your combinations.  If you do need to pool data across species, recognise the species-specific estimates will not be independent because they share common data.  You will need to take care if you wish to make comparisons between estimates that are not independent.  Consult section 3.6.5 of Buckland et al. (2001).
